summary:
South Dakota stands under the United States national framework, and that framework is the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted; passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Within that national frame, South Dakota's own restriction is a facility ban. Governor Larry Rhoden's office announced on Friday 21 March 2025 that he had signed House Bill 1259 the previous day, restricting trans people from using bathrooms matching their gender identity in public schools and state-owned buildings. The measure took effect on 1 July 2025 and marks the first time in state history that a comparable anti-trans bathroom bill has been placed on the books.

The bill's reach is institutional and specific. House Bill 1259 passed the state House by a 49-21 vote and limits restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas in state-run facilities to the same 'biological sex', primarily targeting K-12 schools and state colleges including off-campus activities. Its 'reasonable accommodation' clause and the floor debate raised the prospect that incarcerated trans people would be placed in solitary confinement in order to comply.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 lists South Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults, drawing on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric for the worst bills, and records that federal policies continue to create legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide. The same assessment identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated.
tangentialFactors:
South Dakota's facility law belongs to a wider pattern rather than standing alone. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity; in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban.

Enforcement is no longer theoretical. In April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents are the fastest-moving area of restriction elsewhere in the country. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers; rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions.

Foreign governments have responded publicly. Following the federal document and data rules, multiple countries issued advisories warning their trans citizens about travelling to the United States. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.
localsOnly:
The legislative history indicates durability rather than a one-session accident. Similar legislation failed in South Dakota in 2016, in 2017, twice in 2018 and in 2022 before House Bill 1259 was signed in March 2025.

For residents, the law's practical reach extends beyond school corridors. It governs restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas across state-run facilities, with K-12 schools and state colleges named as the primary targets and off-campus activities covered, and it reaches correctional settings: the 'reasonable accommodation' clause and the House floor debate raised the prospect that incarcerated trans people would be held in solitary confinement to comply with the requirement.

The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map is the reference point for what a resident can obtain, setting out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules a resident encounters depend on the state involved.
outOfScopeNotes:
South Dakota's own rules on changing gender markers on driver's licences and birth certificates are not sourced in this inventory; the Movement Advancement Project map is referenced as the instrument that carries those state-by-state conditions, and South Dakota's specific position on it remains unresolved here.

Whether House Bill 1259 has been challenged in court, and whether any arrest or citation has been recorded under it since it took effect on 1 July 2025, is not sourced in this inventory and should be treated as unresolved.

The inventory names Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel in the 13 July 2026 assessment and gives a total of four such states, but does not state whether South Dakota is among those four; that question is unresolved.

The boundary of 'state-owned buildings' under House Bill 1259, in particular whether privately operated venues, federal facilities or municipal buildings fall inside or outside its scope, is not addressed by the sources available here.
